title: Supervised Learning
text: Supervised learning is a branch of machine learning where a model learns from labeled data, meaning each training example is paired with the correct output. The model learns a mapping from inputs to outputs by minimizing the difference between its predictions and the true labels. Common supervised learning tasks include classification, where the output is a category, and regression, where the output is a continuous value. Popular supervised learning algorithms include linear regression, decision trees, and support vector machines.

title: Unsupervised Learning
text: Unsupervised learning is a branch of machine learning that works with unlabeled data, meaning there are no correct answers provided during training. Instead, the model tries to find hidden structure or patterns within the data on its own. Clustering and dimensionality reduction are two common unsupervised learning tasks. Clustering algorithms group similar data points together, while dimensionality reduction algorithms compress data into fewer features while preserving important structure.

title: Reinforcement Learning
text: Reinforcement learning is a branch of machine learning where an agent learns to make decisions by interacting with an environment. The agent takes actions, observes the resulting state of the environment, and receives a reward signal that tells it how good or bad the action was. Over many interactions, the agent learns a policy that maximizes cumulative reward. Reinforcement learning is commonly used in robotics, game playing, and resource management.

title: Neural Networks
text: A neural network is a machine learning model loosely inspired by the structure of the brain, made up of layers of interconnected units called neurons. Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias term, and passes the result through an activation function. Neural networks with multiple hidden layers are called deep neural networks. By stacking many layers, neural networks can learn increasingly abstract representations of the input data.

title: Gradient Descent
text: Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm used to minimize a loss function by iteratively adjusting a model's parameters. At each step, the algorithm computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to the parameters and updates the parameters in the direction that most reduces the loss. The size of each update is controlled by a hyperparameter called the learning rate. Variants of gradient descent include stochastic gradient descent and mini-batch gradient descent, which use subsets of the training data at each step.

title: Backpropagation
text: Backpropagation is the algorithm used to compute gradients in a neural network so that its weights can be updated with gradient descent. It works by applying the chain rule of calculus, propagating the error from the output layer backward through each hidden layer. At each layer, backpropagation computes how much each weight contributed to the final loss. This makes it possible to train deep neural networks with many layers efficiently.

title: Overfitting
text: Overfitting occurs when a machine learning model learns the training data too closely, including its noise and random fluctuations, rather than the underlying pattern. An overfit model performs very well on training data but poorly on new, unseen data because it fails to generalize. Overfitting is more likely when a model is too complex relative to the amount of training data available. Techniques like regularization, dropout, and early stopping help reduce overfitting.

title: Underfitting
text: Underfitting occurs when a machine learning model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern in the training data. An underfit model performs poorly on both the training data and new data because it has not learned enough structure. Underfitting is often caused by using a model with too little capacity, training for too few iterations, or applying excessive regularization. The remedy for underfitting is usually to increase model complexity or train for longer.

title: Regularization
text: Regularization refers to a set of techniques used to prevent a machine learning model from overfitting by discouraging overly complex solutions. L1 regularization adds a penalty proportional to the absolute value of the model's weights, which can drive some weights to exactly zero. L2 regularization adds a penalty proportional to the square of the weights, which shrinks weights toward zero without eliminating them. Dropout, a regularization technique specific to neural networks, randomly disables a fraction of neurons during training.

title: Cross-Validation
text: Cross-validation is a technique for evaluating how well a machine learning model generalizes to unseen data. In k-fold cross-validation, the training data is split into k equally sized folds. The model is trained on k-1 folds and evaluated on the remaining fold, and this process is repeated k times so every fold serves as the evaluation set once. The final performance estimate is the average across all k runs, which gives a more reliable estimate than a single train-test split.

title: Train-Test Split
text: A train-test split divides a dataset into a portion used to train a machine learning model and a separate portion used to evaluate it. The test set must never be used during training, otherwise the evaluation will be overly optimistic and will not reflect real-world performance. A common practice is to also hold out a validation set, distinct from the test set, used for tuning hyperparameters. Splitting data correctly, before any preprocessing that looks at the whole dataset, is essential to avoid data leakage.

title: Feature Engineering
text: Feature engineering is the process of transforming raw data into features that better represent the underlying problem to a machine learning model. Good features can make a simple model perform well, while poor features can make even a powerful model fail. Common feature engineering techniques include scaling numerical values, encoding categorical variables, and creating new features by combining existing ones. Domain knowledge often plays a large role in designing effective features.

title: Decision Trees
text: A decision tree is a machine learning model that makes predictions by asking a sequence of questions about the input features, splitting the data at each node based on the answer. The tree starts at a root node and branches into child nodes until it reaches leaf nodes, which hold the final predictions. Decision trees are trained by choosing splits that best separate the data according to a criterion such as information gain or Gini impurity. They are easy to interpret but prone to overfitting if grown too deep.

title: Random Forests
text: A random forest is an ensemble of many decision trees, each trained on a random subset of the training data and a random subset of features. The final prediction is made by combining the predictions of all the individual trees, typically by majority vote for classification or averaging for regression. Because each tree sees slightly different data, the errors of individual trees tend to cancel out, making random forests more robust and less prone to overfitting than a single decision tree.

title: Support Vector Machines
text: A support vector machine is a supervised learning model that finds the hyperplane that best separates data points belonging to different classes. The best hyperplane is the one that maximizes the margin, the distance between the hyperplane and the nearest data points from each class, called support vectors. When data is not linearly separable, support vector machines can use a kernel function to map the data into a higher-dimensional space where a separating hyperplane exists.

title: K-Nearest Neighbors
text: K-nearest neighbors is a simple supervised learning algorithm that makes predictions based on the k closest training examples to a given input, according to some distance metric such as Euclidean distance. For classification, the predicted label is the most common label among the k nearest neighbors. For regression, the prediction is the average value of the k nearest neighbors. K-nearest neighbors requires no explicit training phase, but predictions can be slow on large datasets since every prediction requires searching the entire training set.

title: K-Means Clustering
text: K-means clustering is an unsupervised learning algorithm that partitions data into k clusters based on similarity. The algorithm starts by randomly initializing k cluster centers, then alternates between assigning each data point to its nearest cluster center and updating each cluster center to be the mean of the points assigned to it. This process repeats until the cluster assignments stop changing. K-means is sensitive to the initial placement of cluster centers, so it is often run multiple times with different initializations.

title: Principal Component Analysis
text: Principal component analysis, or PCA, is an unsupervised technique for reducing the number of features in a dataset while preserving as much variance as possible. PCA works by finding new axes, called principal components, that are linear combinations of the original features and are ordered by how much variance they explain. Projecting data onto the first few principal components often preserves most of the important structure while significantly reducing dimensionality, which helps with visualization and can reduce overfitting.

title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
text: The bias-variance tradeoff describes the balance between two sources of error in a machine learning model. Bias is the error introduced by approximating a complex real-world problem with a simplified model, and high bias tends to cause underfitting. Variance is the error introduced by a model's sensitivity to small fluctuations in the training data, and high variance tends to cause overfitting. As model complexity increases, bias typically decreases while variance increases, so choosing the right model complexity means finding a balance between the two.

title: Loss Functions
text: A loss function measures how far a machine learning model's predictions are from the true target values, giving a single number that training tries to minimize. Mean squared error is a common loss function for regression tasks, penalizing large errors more heavily than small ones. Cross-entropy loss is a common loss function for classification tasks, penalizing confident predictions that turn out to be wrong. The choice of loss function shapes what kind of mistakes the model is encouraged to avoid during training.

title: Activation Functions
text: An activation function is applied to the output of a neuron in a neural network to introduce non-linearity, allowing the network to learn complex patterns rather than just linear combinations of its inputs. Common activation functions include the sigmoid function, which squashes values between zero and one, and the rectified linear unit, or ReLU, which outputs zero for negative inputs and the input itself for positive inputs. Without activation functions, stacking multiple layers would be mathematically equivalent to a single linear layer.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks
text: A convolutional neural network, or CNN, is a type of neural network commonly used for image data, built around convolutional layers that slide small filters across the input to detect local patterns such as edges and textures. Because the same filter is applied across the entire image, convolutional layers use far fewer parameters than fully connected layers while remaining effective at capturing spatial structure. Pooling layers are often used alongside convolutions to reduce the spatial size of the representation and provide some invariance to small shifts in the input.

title: Recurrent Neural Networks
text: A recurrent neural network, or RNN, is a type of neural network designed for sequential data, where the output at each step depends on both the current input and a hidden state carried over from previous steps. This hidden state acts as a form of memory, allowing the network to model dependencies across time. Traditional RNNs struggle to learn long-range dependencies due to vanishing gradients, which led to the development of variants like long short-term memory networks that are better at retaining information over longer sequences.

title: Attention and Transformers
text: Attention is a mechanism that allows a model to weigh the importance of different parts of its input when producing each part of its output, rather than relying solely on a fixed hidden state. The transformer architecture is built entirely around attention, using self-attention layers to let every position in a sequence directly attend to every other position. This makes transformers highly parallelizable compared to recurrent networks and has made them the dominant architecture for large language models.

title: Embeddings
text: An embedding is a learned, dense vector representation of a discrete object such as a word, so that objects with similar meaning or usage end up close together in the vector space. Embeddings are typically learned by training a model on a task where nearby context predicts useful structure, such as predicting a word from its surrounding words. Once learned, embeddings can be reused as input features for other machine learning models, and distances between embedding vectors often reflect meaningful semantic relationships.

title: Transfer Learning
text: Transfer learning is a technique where a model trained on one task is reused as the starting point for a model on a related task, rather than training a new model from scratch. This is especially useful when the new task has limited labeled data, since the pretrained model has already learned general-purpose features from a larger dataset. A common approach is to freeze most of the pretrained model's layers and only fine-tune the final layers on the new task's data.

title: Hyperparameter Tuning
text: Hyperparameters are configuration values for a machine learning model that are set before training begins, such as the learning rate, the number of layers, or the regularization strength, as opposed to parameters like weights that are learned during training. Hyperparameter tuning is the process of searching for the combination of hyperparameters that yields the best performance on a validation set. Common tuning strategies include grid search, which exhaustively tries every combination, and random search, which samples combinations at random and often finds good settings more efficiently.

title: Ensemble Learning
text: Ensemble learning combines the predictions of multiple machine learning models to produce a final prediction that is often more accurate and robust than any single model alone. Bagging methods, such as random forests, train models independently on different subsets of the data and combine their outputs by averaging or voting. Boosting methods, such as gradient boosting, train models sequentially, where each new model focuses on correcting the errors made by the previous ones.

title: Precision and Recall
text: Precision and recall are two metrics used to evaluate classification models, especially when classes are imbalanced. Precision measures the fraction of positive predictions that are actually correct, while recall measures the fraction of actual positive examples that the model correctly identified. There is often a tradeoff between the two: increasing recall by predicting positive more often tends to lower precision, and vice versa. The F1 score combines precision and recall into a single number using their harmonic mean.

title: Confusion Matrix
text: A confusion matrix is a table that summarizes the performance of a classification model by comparing predicted labels against true labels. Each row typically represents the actual class and each column represents the predicted class, with the diagonal entries showing correct predictions and the off-diagonal entries showing different types of mistakes. From a confusion matrix, metrics like accuracy, precision, and recall can all be derived, and it is especially useful for spotting which specific classes a model tends to confuse with each other.
